versions.label: BSB
paragraphs: 1 After two full years had passed, Pharaoh had a dream: He was standing beside the Nile, 2 when seven cows, sleek and well-fed, came up from the river and began to graze among the reeds. 3 After them, seven other cows, sickly and thin, came up from the Nile and stood beside the well-fed cows on the bank of the river. 4 And the cows that were sickly and thin devoured the seven sleek, well-fed cows.

Then Pharaoh woke up, 5 but he fell back asleep and dreamed a second time: Seven heads of grain, plump and ripe, came up on one stalk. 6 After them, seven other heads of grain sprouted, thin and scorched by the east wind. 7 And the thin heads of grain swallowed up the seven plump, ripe ones. Then Pharaoh awoke and realized it was a dream.
8 In the morning his spirit was troubled, so he summoned all the magicians and wise men of Egypt. Pharaoh told them his dreams, but no one could interpret them for him.

9 Then the chief cupbearer said to Pharaoh, “Today I recall my failures. 10 Pharaoh was once angry with his servants, and he put me and the chief baker in the custody of the captain of the guard. 11 One night both the chief baker and I had dreams, and each dream had its own meaning. 12 Now a young Hebrew was there with us, a servant of the captain of the guard. We told him our dreams and he interpreted them for us individually. 13 And it happened to us just as he had interpreted: I was restored to my position, and the other man was hanged.”

context_lines: Two full years pass after the cupbearer returns to Pharaoh's service. Joseph remains in prison. The narrative marks the delay before describing the event that finally brings his name before the king: Pharaoh has two dreams that trouble him.

In the first, seven healthy cows come out of the Nile, followed by seven gaunt cows that eat them. In the second, seven full heads of grain are swallowed by seven thin heads scorched by the east wind. The repeated movement from abundance to something that consumes it makes the dreams disturbing, but their meaning has not yet been explained.

Pharaoh summons Egypt's magicians and wise men, but none can interpret the dreams for him. The cupbearer then recalls his earlier failures and tells Pharaoh about the young Hebrew who interpreted the prison dreams. He can report a result the king's court can recognize: one official was restored, and the other was hanged, exactly as Joseph had said.

The forgotten prisoner is now recommended because of a specific, tested experience. The chapter has not yet shown his release, but the failure of Pharaoh's advisers and the cupbearer's recollection bring the story to the threshold of a sudden change.
common_interpretation_lines: A common Christian reading sees God bringing the earlier prison encounter into use at the moment Pharaoh needs an answer. [Wesley's notes on Genesis 41:8–9](https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-first-book-of-moses-called-genesis/) emphasize the failure of the royal advisers and the timing of Joseph's eventual opportunity. The two-year interval makes clear that the answer comes after a substantial wait.
current_position_lines: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.
god_plan_lines: The delay and the new opportunity belong to the same longer story. [Psalm 105:19–22](https://biblehub.com/bsb/psalms/105.htm) describes Joseph waiting until his prediction comes true, then being released and placed in authority. What the cupbearer had forgotten becomes relevant again when Pharaoh cannot obtain an answer elsewhere.

God's preparation here reaches beyond improving Joseph's circumstances. The coming famine will threaten many people, including Jacob's household. [Acts 7:9–14](https://biblehub.com/bsb/acts/7.htm) later joins Joseph's rescue and appointment with the family's need for food and its move to Egypt. His long-awaited opening is part of provision for others as well as release for himself.
